# US county data, 2000–2024

Economic, demographic, and political data for every county in the United
States: 50 variables covering population, age, race and
ethnicity, poverty, income, employment, education, housing, and presidential
elections. The data was assembled by CS765 course staff from public federal
statistical sources (see [Sources](#sources)). State-level and national
totals are included too, so you can explore the data at several levels of
aggregation.

The same data comes in several shapes, so you can pick the one that suits
your tools and questions.

## Quick start

- **One row per county, few columns** (good for maps and scatterplots):
  `county_wide_compact_snapshot.csv`.
- **Change over time** (good for line charts, small multiples, animation):
  `county_panel.csv` (tall), or `county_wide_compact.csv` (wide).
- **States instead of counties**: the `state_*` files.
- **What does a column mean?** See [Column reference](#column-reference) below,
  or `variables.csv`.

Read the `fips` column as **text**, not a number. It is a 5-digit code with
meaningful leading zeros: `01001` is Autauga County, Alabama, but as a number
it becomes `1001`, which no longer matches other data sources (or map files).
In pandas use `pd.read_csv(..., dtype={"fips": str})`. In Excel or Tableau,
set the column type to text/string.

| `county_wide_compact.csv` | wide | 28 core | every year, 2000–2024 | 3,236 × 589 | 10.3 MB |

| `state_wide_snapshot.csv` | wide | all 49 | election years, 2000–2024 | 53 × 300 | 0.1 MB |
| `state_wide_compact_snapshot.csv` | wide | 27 core | election years, 2000–2024 | 53 × 170 | 55 KB |

What the file names mean:

- **panel** (tall): one row per county per year. Each variable is a single
  column, e.g. `poverty_rate`, and the `year` column says which year a row is
  for. Rows exist only for years where the county has some data.
- **wide**: one row per county. Each variable/year pair is its own column,
  named `<variable>_<year>`, e.g. `poverty_rate_2016`. A column exists only if
  there is data for that variable in that year.
- **compact**: only the core variables (marked "yes" in the "Core" column of
  the reference below), mostly rates and percentages, plus `population` and
  `votes_total` so you can weight when aggregating.
- **snapshot**: only presidential election years (2000, 2004, ..., 2024),
  which keeps wide files to a manageable number of columns.
- **state_\***: the same structures for the 50 states, the District of
  Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the United States as a whole (`fips` = `00000`,
  `state` = `US`). They have no `county_name` or `median_age`, and their only
  geography column is `land_area_sqmi`. The US total excludes Puerto Rico.
- **variables.csv**: the column reference below as a spreadsheet: one row
  per variable with its description, units, source, years covered, and
  notes.

## Identifying columns

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `fips` | 5-digit FIPS code: 2-digit state code + 3-digit county code. The unique ID for a county; names are not unique (31 counties and parishes are named Washington). State rows use `SS000`, the US uses `00000`. |
| `state` | Two-letter postal abbreviation, e.g. `WI`. |
| `state_name` | Full state name. |
| `county_name` | County name, e.g. `Dane County`. |
| `region` | Census region: Northeast, Midwest, South, or West. Blank for Puerto Rico. |
| `division` | Census division (9 groups of states, e.g. East North Central), nested within regions. Blank for Puerto Rico. |
| `year` | Year the values refer to (tall files only; in wide files the year is part of the column name). |

"Counties" includes county equivalents: parishes in Louisiana, boroughs and
census areas in Alaska, independent cities in Virginia (plus Baltimore,
St. Louis, and Carson City), the District of Columbia, municipios in Puerto
Rico, and Connecticut's planning regions.

## Column reference

Percentages run from 0 to 100. Rates are per 1,000 people. Dollar amounts are
**not adjusted for inflation**, so $50,000 in 2000 bought much more than
$50,000 in 2024. "Years" lists the years with data in these files.

### Population and population change

| Column | Description | Units | Years | Core | Source | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `population` | Population (July 1 estimate) | persons | 2000–2024 | yes | Census PEP | 2000-2019 use the Census Bureau's revised (intercensal) estimates, so there is no artificial jump at 2010 or 2020. |
| `population_density` | Population per square mile of land | persons/sq mi | 2000–2024 | yes | Census PEP + Gazetteer | population / land_area_sqmi. Uses current land area for every year. |
| `births` | Births during the year ending July 1 | persons | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | Census PEP | Year ending July 1. Missing for 2000, 2010, 2020: in census years the estimates cover only April-July. |
| `deaths` | Deaths during the year ending July 1 | persons | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | Census PEP | As for births. |
| `natural_change` | Births minus deaths | persons | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | Census PEP | As for births. |
| `international_migration` | Net international migration | persons | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | Census PEP | As for births. |
| `domestic_migration` | Net domestic (within-US) migration | persons | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | Census PEP | As for births. |
| `net_migration` | Net migration (international + domestic) | persons | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | Census PEP | As for births. |
| `birth_rate` | Birth rate | per 1,000 people | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | yes | derived | births / population x 1000. |
| `death_rate` | Death rate | per 1,000 people | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | yes | derived | deaths / population x 1000. |
| `natural_change_rate` | Natural change rate | per 1,000 people | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | derived | natural_change / population x 1000. |
| `international_migration_rate` | International migration rate | per 1,000 people | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | derived | international_migration / population x 1000. |
| `domestic_migration_rate` | Domestic migration rate | per 1,000 people | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | | derived | domestic_migration / population x 1000. Negative = more people moved out. |
| `net_migration_rate` | Net migration rate | per 1,000 people | 2001–2009, 2011–2019, 2021–2024 | yes | derived | net_migration / population x 1000. |

## Things to watch out for

- **Not every variable exists for every year.** Blank means "no data", not
  zero. Check the table above before comparing years.
- **Counties change.** Connecticut replaced its 8 counties with 9 "planning
  regions" in 2022. Most sources switch to the new units around 2020–2022,
  but employment data uses the planning regions for every year. As a result
  the old counties and the new regions each appear only for some years and
  some variables. Other changes: Bedford city, Virginia merged into Bedford
  County in 2013; several Alaska areas were split or merged; Broomfield
  County, Colorado was created in 2001 (some sources fill in earlier years,
  others don't). A county that appears or disappears
  partway through almost always had a boundary or code change, not a sudden
  change in population.
- **Births, deaths, and migration are blank for 2000, 2010, and 2020.** In
  census years the Census Bureau's estimates cover only April–July, so values
  would look artificially small.
- **Survey averages.** Education (from 2009), housing, foreign-born, and the
  Gini index come from the American Community Survey. Each value averages 5
  years of survey responses and is labeled by the last year: "2024" means
  2020–2024. Neighboring years share 4 of their 5 years, so changes are
  smoothed and lag real events, and small counties have large margins of
  error.
- **Education before 2009** comes from the 2000 census, so in the snapshot
  files there is a gap between 2000 and 2012.
- **Model estimates.** Poverty and median household income are statistical
  model estimates, also uncertain for small counties.
- **Big events show up.** 2020 unemployment reflects the COVID-19 pandemic;
  2005–2006 has missing employment data for some Louisiana parishes after
  Hurricane Katrina.
- **Virginia** has many small independent cities. The personal income data
  lumps most of them with a neighboring county, so they have no
  `personal_income` or `per_capita_income`.
- **Elections**: there is no county-level data for Alaska (it reports results
  by legislative district). Kansas City, Missouri reports separately; its votes
  are included in Jackson County. Vote shares for the Democratic and
  Republican candidates do not add to 100 because of third-party candidates.
- **Puerto Rico** is only covered by some sources (employment and the survey
  variables), and it is not part of the US totals.
- **Small numbers are noisy.** The smallest counties have under 100 residents,
  so their rates and percentages jump around. Consider filtering or weighting
  by population.

## Aggregating counties

To combine counties into states, regions, or your own groups:

- **Counts add up**: `population`, `births`, `unemployed`, `votes_total`, and
  so on.
- **Percentages and rates must be weighted**: multiply by the population they
  describe, add up, then divide by the total. For example, a region's
  `pct_dem` = sum of (`pct_dem` × `votes_total`) ÷ sum of `votes_total`. The
  right weight is the variable's universe: `labor_force` for unemployment,
  `adults_25_plus` for education, `votes_total` for vote shares. `population` is
  a reasonable approximation for the others.
- **Medians cannot be combined** (`median_age`, `median_household_income`,
  `median_home_value`, `median_gross_rent`), and neither can `gini_index`. A
  population-weighted average of county medians is only a rough
  approximation.
- **Check your work** against the `state_*` files. For counts and
  percentages, the state values were computed from the counties, so they
  should match. For poverty, household income, personal income, housing
  values, and the Gini index, the state files use the sources' own state
  estimates, which come from separate statistical models and will differ a
  little from anything you compute from counties.

## Sources

The "Source" column in the reference uses these abbreviations:

- **Census PEP**: US Census Bureau, Population Estimates Program. Population,
  births, deaths, migration, age, race and ethnicity.
- **Census SAIPE**: US Census Bureau, Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates.
  Poverty and median household income.
- **Census ACS 5-year**: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year
  estimates. Education (2009 on), housing, foreign-born, Gini index.
- **Census Gazetteer**: US Census Bureau Gazetteer files. Land area, latitude,
  longitude.
- **BLS LAUS**: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment
  Statistics. Labor force and unemployment.
- **BEA CAINC1**: Bureau of Economic Analysis, Regional Economic Accounts,
  table CAINC1. Personal income.
- **USDA ERS**: USDA Economic Research Service. Education 1970–2000 (from the
  decennial census); Rural-Urban Continuum Codes and Urban Influence Codes.
- **MIT Election Lab**: MIT Election Data and Science Lab, County Presidential
  Election Returns 2000–2024, Harvard Dataverse,
  <https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/VOQCHQ>.
- **derived**: computed by course staff from the other columns, as described
  in the notes.

All source data was downloaded in October 2026 and combined by course staff
for CS765 at UW–Madison. Sources revise their estimates over time, so values
may differ slightly from what their websites show today.
